Insider Trading: A Love Letter to the People Who Still Believe in the Tooth Fairy of “Fair Markets”

Every society has its sacred myths.

The ancient Greeks had Zeus.
The Middle Ages had dragons.
And modern finance has “the level playing field.”

You know the people who worship this myth. They write outraged think-pieces about insider trading while calmly ignoring everything else that actually happens in markets. To them, insider trading is the Final Boss of Financial Evil, far worse than, say, massive high-frequency trading operations front-running their orders by nanoseconds from a server literally inside the exchange.

No, no. That’s “liquidity provision.”

Insider trading is the real monster, because Karen from Ohio might buy a stock at $47 when — gasp — someone else already knows it should really be $49.

Call the Hague.

The Romantic Belief in the Virgin-Born Market

Opponents of legalizing insider trading cling to the idea that markets are supposed to be “fair.”

That’s adorable.

They’ll say, “Everyone should have equal access to information!” as they:

  • Trade on tips from CNBC talking heads with massive conflicts of interest
  • Read reports from analysts who are literally being wined and dined by the companies they cover
  • Buy into IPOs where insiders already priced them, allocated them, and briefed a dozen “special clients” before your brokerage app even updated

But this is all fine. It’s only when someone inside the company uses information accurately and early that suddenly we must defend the sanctity of the retail trader.

You know, the same retail trader who just spent $800 on an options YOLO because a Reddit thread had a lot of fire emojis.

“Information Asymmetry Is Bad” … Except for All the Ones We Like

Critics love the phrase “information asymmetry.” They say it like a priest saying “heresy.”

But somehow, they’re completely unbothered by:

  • Hedge funds paying for alternative data: satellite images of parking lots, credit card swipes, app usage patterns
  • Institutional investors getting private meetings with management while retail investors squint at quarterly slides on their phone
  • High-frequency traders co-locating servers in the same building as the exchange so they can react faster than your broker’s login screen loads

All of that is… what’s the word… “sophistication.”

Yet if an executive who actually knows what’s going on with the company uses that information in a trade, it’s suddenly the moral equivalent of kicking a puppy.

So, to summarize the orthodoxy:

  • Pay millions for obscure data: “Smart!”
  • Hire a lobbyist to shape regulation in your favor: “Strategic!”
  • Talk privately to management before everyone else: “Relationship-building!”
  • Actually be management and trade on what you know: “CRIMINAL MONSTER RUINING TRUST IN MARKETS.”

“But It’s Not Fair to Small Investors!”

Opponents love to pretend they’re defending “the little guy.”

This is the same “little guy” who:

  • Trades biotech penny stocks based on a TikTok video
  • Buys at the peak of every hype cycle and sells at the bottom because “it dropped 10% and I panicked”
  • Thinks reading one bullish blog post is “due diligence”

We’re supposed to believe this person is being grievously harmed because an insider sold shares at $52.30 instead of $51.90 before the earnings call?

If your investment strategy can be completely undone by someone else knowing more than you, I have bad news: you are already doomed in the actual market, where everyone is trying to know more than you, faster than you, with better tools than you.

The outrage is like complaining that Olympic sprinters have an unfair advantage because they train.

The “Trust in Markets” Argument

Another favorite: “If insider trading is allowed, people will lose trust in markets!”

Right. Because currently:

  • Companies can legally be wildly optimistic on earnings calls
  • Analysts can be wrong 80% of the time and remain employed
  • Market crashes wipe out years of gains in a few hours, and the explanation is “sentiment shifted”
  • Meme stocks detach from reality entirely and then crater, leaving retail bagholders wondering what just happened

But no, the public’s trust would be shattered by learning that some trades were based on accurate and timely information instead of vibes, rumors, and lagging data.

We must preserve the illusion that everyone is equal at the casino. Sure, the house has algorithms, comps the whales, and sees everyone’s cards, but technically you and your $500 are “participating in free markets.”

Hero Worship of Regulators

Opponents talk about insider trading enforcement as if regulators are a squad of Avengers protecting the innocent.

Reality: enforcement is:

  • Sporadic
  • Politically selective
  • Totally incapable of catching all but the dumbest offenders

It’s like trying to police speeding by ticketing only those who drive exactly 101 mph on Tuesdays.

But critics love this. They adore the symbolic comfort: “Someone, somewhere, is occasionally punished. That means the system is fair.”

If you legalized insider trading, what happens? The pretense drops. You’d have to admit that markets are:

  • Messy
  • Unequal
  • Driven by information disparities

Which, by the way, they already are. The only difference is that we currently pretend some types of information advantage are polite and others are obscene.

The Moral Panic

Let’s be honest: most outrage about insider trading is vibes-based.

“Insider trading feels wrong.”
“Someone had an unfair advantage.”
“It just doesn’t seem ethical.”

None of this outrage extends to:

  • Lobbyists writing industry-friendly regulation
  • Corporate executives announcing layoffs after their stock vests
  • Politicians trading stocks in sectors they regulate, perfectly “legally” because they used the public loophole form instead of a phone call

Those are somehow just “complicated issues.”

But if an engineer sees that the product is a disaster and sells shares three days before the press release? That’s the line. That’s what destroys civilization.

Imagine the Transparency if It Were Legal

Legalizing insider trading wouldn’t make markets “unfair.” They already are. It would just:

  • Make it obvious who actually believes in their own company
  • Accelerate price discovery: stock prices would reflect real information faster
  • Expose corporate nonsense quicker, because insiders with truth-based incentives would sell early and often

Opponents claim this would “scare people away from markets.” Translation: “People might realize the fairy tale was a fairy tale and stop pretending we’re all equal in a system explicitly designed not to be.”

Can’t have that.

Conclusion: Protect the Illusion at All Costs

People who oppose legalizing insider trading aren’t defending fairness. They’re defending the feeling of fairness — the comforting bedtime story that everyone has a shot, even though:

  • Capital, connections, and data already decide the game
  • Large players already operate with massive informational advantages
  • “Legal” isn’t the same thing as “balanced”

Insider trading is just the one advantage they’ve decided to label “immoral,” not because it’s uniquely harmful, but because it punctures the fantasy too directly.

So we’re left with a system where:

  • Hidden advantages are fine
  • Sophisticated advantages are fine
  • Algorithmic advantages are fine
  • Government-influenced advantages are fine
  • But straightforward “I know more because I actually work here” is forbidden in the name of “optics.”

Opponents of legalization don’t want fair markets. They want markets that look fair enough that no one asks too many questions.

And if that requires demonizing the one group of traders who actually know what’s going on?

Well, for the sake of the myth, they’ll happily do it.

Ladies and gentlemen,

We stand today at a strange crossroads in the history of markets.

On one side, we claim to worship efficiency, innovation, and freedom. We celebrate “smart money,” rapid information flow, real-time pricing, and rational decision-making.

On the other side, we criminalize one of the most direct, powerful mechanisms for achieving those goals: insider trading.

It is time to end this contradiction. It is time to fully legalize insider trading—not as a loophole, not as a tolerated gray area, but as a legitimate, open, and integral part of how markets process information.

Information Is the Lifeblood of Markets

Every serious economist agrees: information is what makes markets work.

Prices are not magic. They are signals. They are the compressed messages of millions of decisions about risk, value, and expectation. The faster and more accurately prices reflect reality, the healthier the market and the better the allocation of capital.

But what is insider trading, at its core?

It is simply trading on better information.

We already allow and celebrate this in countless forms:

  • Analysts build models with proprietary data.
  • Hedge funds deploy alternative data—satellite images of parking lots, credit card flows, web scraping.
  • Corporate executives give “guidance” that is vague and selectively shared in practice.
  • Large institutions wield research teams that retail investors will never match.

We do not call this “unfair” in a legal sense; we call it “sophistication.” We praise it as expertise, edge, and intelligence.

Yet when the person who actually knows the company best—the insider—acts on that knowledge through trading, we suddenly decide this is intolerable? We declare it a crime, not because it harms the company’s fundamentals, but because it challenges a myth: the myth that everyone can or should have identical information at the same time.

That myth is not only false—it is destructive.

Legalizing Insider Trading Means Faster, Better Prices

Ask a simple question: What happens to markets when insiders are allowed to trade freely on their information?

Prices adjust sooner.

If insiders know that:

  • Earnings will be far better than expected,
  • A life-changing drug trial has succeeded,
  • A disastrous strategic decision has been reversed,

and they can legally buy or sell shares based on that knowledge, prices begin reflecting those realities earlier.

That means:

  • Fewer shocks when “news” finally hits the public.
  • Less violent volatility around announcement dates.
  • More continuous, smoother incorporation of information into prices.

Right now, our regulatory regime forces markets to remain ignorant, even when people with real knowledge are standing right there, forbidden to transmit that knowledge in the most honest language markets understand: buying and selling.

Legal insider trading is not about secrecy. Quite the opposite. It is about creating a powerful incentive for those who know the truth to move prices in the direction of that truth, sooner rather than later.

The Illusion of “Fairness”

The primary argument against insider trading is that it is “unfair.” But we must ask: unfair compared to what?

Markets have never been and will never be information-equal. They are arenas of comparative advantage:

  • Some people have more experience.
  • Some have better data.
  • Some have deeper industry knowledge.
  • Some have more time to analyze.

We do not outlaw expertise. We do not outlaw intelligence. We do not outlaw hard work. Yet we single out one category of superior knowledge—insider knowledge—as illegitimate.

Why? Not because it creates harm in any concrete, measurable sense, but because it offends a sentimental notion that all traders should stand on identical ground.

But that is not how markets function in reality.

Even more ironic: the current regime protects the illusion of fairness while entrenching actual inequality. Large institutions can get as close to insider-level information as possible without crossing an invisible line. They can attend private meetings, read between the lines, infer what’s coming. Retail investors are still last in line. The system pretends to shield them while leaving them chronically behind.

Legalizing insider trading does not make markets “perfectly fair.” Nothing will. But it does make them more honest: prices move when and because people with the best knowledge act, not when a press release finally cleanses the conscience of compliance departments.

Freedom and Responsibility in Economic Decision-Making

There is a deeper philosophical issue at stake: economic freedom.

In a free society, individuals should have the right to make decisions based on what they know—especially when their actions do not violate contracts, do not steal property, and do not coerce anyone.

When we criminalize insider trading, we are saying to informed individuals:

> “You are required to pretend ignorance. You are forbidden from acting rationally on what you know. You must leave prices wrong, capital misallocated, and decisions distorted because the state has decided that your information advantage is morally unacceptable.”

This is not freedom. It is enforced irrationality.

We assume that if insiders are allowed to trade, they will somehow “exploit” the public. But remember: every trade has two sides. If the insider knows that a company is overvalued and sells, the new buyer pays a slightly more accurate price than they would have if insider trading were banned. The loss they might suffer later—when the bad news eventually comes out—is minimized by the earlier adjustment.

Legal insider trading does not guarantee that every individual trade is profitable or that every outsider avoids loss. That is not and never has been the promise of markets. What it does is improve the aggregate accuracy of prices, which benefits everyone who participates over time.

From Policing Trades to Requiring Transparency

The current system channels enormous regulatory energy into a losing game: trying to police who knew what, when, and what counts as “material” non-public information.

  • Vast investigative resources are spent reconstructing conversations.
  • People are prosecuted not for fraud, but for using true information.
  • Companies over-lawyer every communication out of fear.

Imagine redirecting that energy toward genuine transparency and governance instead:

  • Require insiders to disclose their trades in near real-time.
  • Let the market see when insiders are buying aggressively or selling heavily.
  • Make those disclosures easily accessible to all investors.

Now the trades themselves become a public signal:

  • Insider buying? The market infers improving prospects.
  • Insider selling? The market infers caution.

Instead of banning insider trading, we could shine a brighter light on it. Rather than pretend insiders are not trading on information, we accept reality—and regulate it openly, with disclosure, rather than prohibition.

The Hypocrisy of Selective Outrage

Consider the contradictions we live with:

We accept that:

  • Venture capitalists invest based on privileged access to private company information.
  • Private equity firms negotiate deals with deeply asymmetric information.
  • M&A negotiations are driven by insiders on both sides with superior knowledge.

But the moment that same logic reaches the public market, we suddenly cry “fraud,” even when no deception has occurred.

Insider trading laws do not protect us from lies. Fraud is already illegal and should remain illegal. If an insider fabricates information, misleads shareholders, or falsifies data, that is criminal and should be punished severely.

But trading on true information, without lying to anyone, without altering the facts, should not be a crime. It should be recognized as what it is: the most direct way to move prices toward reality.

Embracing an Honest, Efficient Market

Legalizing insider trading is not about saying insiders are heroes or saints. It is about designing institutions that harness human incentives to serve the broader function of markets: discovering prices, directing capital, and rewarding good decisions.

What do we achieve if we fully legalize insider trading in a framework of strong anti-fraud rules and robust disclosure?

  • Faster information flow. Important truths reach prices sooner via trades.
  • More efficient markets. Prices more quickly reflect all available information, not just what’s been sanitized for a press release.
  • Freer economic decision-making. Individuals are not forced to act as if they are ignorant when they are not.
  • More honest regulation. We focus on deception and fraud, not on the mere possession of knowledge.

The alternative is what we have now:

  • A system that pretends to equalize information but never will.
  • A system that criminalizes rational action while tolerating far deeper structural inequities.
  • A system that slows the flow of truth into prices in the name of protecting investors, while often leaving those same investors exposed to delayed shocks.

A Call to Reconsider

This is not a call for anarchy. It is a call for a more coherent, honest, and freedom-consistent financial system.

Keep fraud illegal. Strengthen penalties for falsifying data, misleading investors, or hiding conflicts of interest. But stop criminalizing the simple act of trading on what you genuinely know.

Legalizing insider trading will not make markets perfect. Nothing will. But it will make them faster, clearer, and more aligned with the fundamental purpose of markets: to translate information into prices so that millions of individuals, with their own goals and values, can make better decisions.

It is time to trust information. It is time to trust incentives. It is time to stop pretending that ignorance equals fairness.

It is time to fully legalize insider trading—and let markets do what they do best: discover the truth.

Title: The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Unleashing Market Efficiency through Rapid Information Diffusion

Introduction

The prohibition of insider trading has long been a cornerstone of securities regulation worldwide, rooted in concerns about fairness and the protection of investors. However, a closer examination of the economic dynamics underlying capital markets reveals a different perspective. This essay argues that fully legalizing insider trading would significantly enhance market efficiency by accelerating the incorporation of private information into stock prices. By embracing the free flow of material non-public information, markets can achieve more accurate pricing, reduce volatility, and allocate capital more effectively—benefiting investors, corporations, and the economy as a whole.

The Efficiency of Information Transmission

At the heart of any well-functioning market is the rapid and accurate dissemination of information. The Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) posits that asset prices reflect all available information. In its semi-strong form, prices adjust quickly to publicly disclosed data. Yet, some information—such as upcoming product breakthroughs, merger negotiations, or financial results—remains private until officially released. When insiders (e.g., executives, employees, or advisors) are barred from trading on this knowledge, its diffusion into market prices is delayed until the public announcement. Legalizing insider trading would enable insiders to act on their private information, causing trades that move prices in the direction of the eventual public revelation. This preemptive price adjustment means that by the time the information becomes public, the market price already incorporates it, leading to a smoother and more efficient transition.

Accelerating Price Discovery

Price discovery is the process by which the market determines the appropriate value of a security based on available information. Insiders possess the most accurate and timely information about a company’s prospects. When they are free to trade, their actions serve as powerful signals that guide other participants. For example, if an insider knows that a pharmaceutical firm’s clinical trial has succeeded, buying shares will push the price upward, reflecting the increased expected future cash flows. Other investors, observing the price movement, may infer that positive news is forthcoming and adjust their valuations accordingly. This cascade effect embeds the private information into the price much faster than waiting for an official press release. As a result, the market price becomes a more faithful representation of the company’s true value at any given moment.

Reducing Volatility and Market Shocks

The current ban on insider trading often leads to abrupt price changes when private information is finally disclosed. Markets experience a “jump” as they digest the news, which can cause unnecessary volatility and panic. Legal insider trading would spread these adjustments over a longer period, smoothing the price path. Insiders would trade gradually, avoiding the stampede that typically accompanies a surprise announcement. This gradual incorporation of information reduces the risk of extreme volatility, making markets more stable and attractive to a broader range of investors, including risk-averse participants.

Aligning Incentives and Encouraging Entrepreneurship

Insider trading prohibitions create a wedge between the interests of insiders and shareholders. Executives and employees, who are often compensated with equity, cannot fully capitalize on their insights into company performance. This misalignment may dampen their motivation to innovate and take calculated risks. Legalizing insider trading would allow these key stakeholders to profit from their superior knowledge, aligning their incentives more closely with those of shareholders. The prospect of personal gain from successful ventures could spur entrepreneurial spirit, encouraging management to pursue value-creating projects with greater vigor.

Enhancing Capital Allocation

Efficient capital allocation is a fundamental benefit of well-functioning financial markets. When prices accurately reflect firm-specific information, resources flow to their most productive uses. Companies with promising prospects see their stock prices rise, making equity financing cheaper and enabling them to invest in growth. Conversely, firms with declining prospects experience price declines, signaling the need for restructuring or exit. Insider trading accelerates this signaling process, leading to a more dynamic and adaptive economy.

Addressing Counterarguments: Fairness and Asymmetry

Critics contend that insider trading is unfair to ordinary investors who lack access to private information. However, fairness in this context is often misunderstood. All market participants operate with varying degrees of information; some rely on superior research, analytical models, or intuition. Legalizing insider trading does not create a new inequality—it simply acknowledges that insiders have unique insights and allows them to share that knowledge through trading. Moreover, the overall benefit to market efficiency outweighs the perceived disadvantage to any individual investor, as the latter still enjoys the advantages of more accurate pricing and reduced volatility.

Another concern is that insider trading could encourage information hoarding and reduce transparency. Yet, the very act of trading on private information forces its partial disclosure. The price signal itself conveys information, even if the exact details remain hidden. In fact, a market where insiders are free to trade is more transparent in the sense that prices adjust earlier, giving all participants a clearer picture of a company’s trajectory.

Conclusion

Legalizing insider trading is a bold but economically sound reform that would unlock significant gains in market efficiency. By enabling the swift integration of private information into stock prices, we foster a more accurate, stable, and dynamic pricing mechanism. This, in turn, improves capital allocation, aligns managerial incentives, and ultimately strengthens the economy. Rather than viewing insider trading as a moral hazard, policymakers should recognize its potential as a powerful tool for information dissemination. The time has come to discard outdated prohibitions and embrace a regulatory framework that harnesses the full power of market forces—where every participant, insider or not, benefits from the wisdom of prices.

Introduction

Insider trading – the buying or selling of a company’s securities by individuals with access to non-public, material information – is illegal in most jurisdictions, including the United States under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. However, from a free-market economics perspective, some scholars and advocates argue that legalizing insider trading could enhance price discovery and overall market efficiency. This explanation outlines the theoretical benefits and reasoning behind that position, focusing on how insider trading might improve information dissemination and resource allocation.

1. Price Discovery through Faster Information Incorporation

Price discovery is the process by which market prices reflect all available information relevant to an asset’s value. In an efficient market, prices adjust rapidly as new information emerges. Insider trading can accelerate this adjustment because insiders, armed with private information, trade in ways that move the market price toward its “true” value before that information becomes public.

For example, if a corporate executive knows that a forthcoming product will exceed expectations, they can buy shares before the news is released. Their buying pressure pushes the price up, partially incorporating the positive information. Other investors, observing the price movement and inferring that someone with superior knowledge is buying, may adjust their valuations, further refining the price. When the public announcement finally occurs, the price move is smaller because the information was already anticipated. This leads to a smoother, more continuous price adjustment process, reducing volatility around news events.

Legalizing insider trading thus allows private information to be transmitted to the market through the most direct channel – actual trades – rather than waiting for slower, often bureaucratic, public disclosure processes. This results in prices that are more accurate reflections of underlying fundamentals at any given time.

2. Enhanced Market Efficiency

Market efficiency refers to the ability of markets to allocate capital to its highest-valued uses. Accurate prices are crucial because they serve as signals for investors and companies about where to invest, produce, or divest. When prices incorporate information quickly, capital flows more swiftly to promising opportunities and away from unproductive ones, increasing overall economic welfare.

Insider trading improves efficiency in several ways:

  • Reduced information asymmetry: While insider trading is often criticized for exploiting information gaps, its legalization could actually reduce asymmetry over time. As insiders trade, their actions become visible in the order flow and price changes, allowing other market participants to infer that something important is happening. This encourages outside investors and analysts to engage in their own research, increasing the overall depth of market information.

  • Lower costs of information production: If insiders are allowed to profit from their private knowledge, they have a stronger incentive to gather and act on valuable information. This can lead to more thorough monitoring of corporate performance and earlier detection of problems. The market then benefits from the “early warning” signals without having to pay for the information directly.

  • Better resource allocation: With more accurate prices, companies can raise capital at fairer valuations, and investors can make more informed decisions. Resources are less likely to be misdirected to firms with hidden weaknesses or overvalued prospects.

3. Aligned Incentives and Compensation

From a free-market standpoint, insider trading can serve as an efficient form of performance-based compensation, especially for startups and knowledge-intensive firms where cash compensation is limited. Allowing executives and key employees to trade on inside information gives them a direct stake in the company’s success, aligning their interests with shareholders. This “insider trading as compensation” argument suggests that bans force firms to rely on less effective or more costly incentive mechanisms (e.g., stock options with restrictive vesting schedules).

Moreover, the possibility of profiting from superior information can motivate managers to work harder, take calculated risks, and stay vigilant about competitive threats – behaviors that benefit shareholders and the broader economy.

4. Victimless and Voluntary Transactions

A core free-market principle is that voluntary exchanges between consenting parties should be permitted unless they cause harm to others. Critics claim insider trading harms uninformed investors, but proponents argue that sellers in insider transactions (e.g., an employee selling shares to an insider) do so willingly at market prices. No one is coerced, and the seller could have sold at the same price to anyone else. The buyer simply possesses better information and is willing to pay the prevailing price; the trade itself does not inflict harm. Thus, the prohibition is seen as an unnecessary restriction on peaceful commerce.

5. Avoidance of Distortions and Enforcement Costs

Banning insider trading creates a black market for information, leading to costly enforcement efforts and the risk of punitive measures that may inadvertently penalize innocent market participants. Legalization would eliminate these distortions, allowing market forces to regulate the practice naturally. For instance, excessive insider trading that manipulates prices would still be illegal under anti-fraud statutes; but routine, non-deceptive trading on private information would be treated as any other market activity.

Conclusion

From a free-market economics perspective, legalizing insider trading is argued to improve price discovery by embedding private information into market prices more swiftly, thereby enhancing overall market efficiency. The alleged benefits include faster information incorporation, reduced information asymmetry, stronger incentives for information gathering, efficient compensation, and adherence to voluntary exchange principles. While the policy remains controversial and faces significant legal and ethical objections, the theoretical case rests on the belief that markets function best when information flows freely and participants are allowed to act on their knowledge without government interference.

The debate over insider trading has long been mired in controversy, with a prevailing sentiment that it is an unethical, if not illegal, practice that undermines the fairness of financial markets. Understanding Market Efficiency

Market efficiency, a cornerstone concept in finance, posits that asset prices should reflect all available information at any given time. This ideal state, often referred to as the efficient market hypothesis, implies that investors cannot consistently earn abnormal returns by trading on publicly available data alone. However, in reality, markets are not perfectly efficient. Insider trading, when legalized, can act as a bridge across this information divide. Insiders, by virtue of their positions within a company, have access to highly relevant and often proprietary information that is not yet available to the general public. This information could range from pending product launches, significant contract wins, or even early indicators of financial distress. When insiders are permitted to trade on this knowledge, they are effectively injecting their private insights directly into the market.

Introduction

For decades, insider trading has been vilified as a form of market manipulation that unfairly advantages the few at the expense of the many. The Efficiency Argument: Faster and More Accurate Price Discovery

The most compelling argument for legalizing insider trading lies in its contribution to market efficiency. Stock prices serve as crucial signals in our economy, guiding capital allocation and corporate decision-making. The more quickly and accurately these prices reflect all available information—including insider information—the better our markets function.

When insiders trade on private information, they move stock prices toward their true value more rapidly than would otherwise occur. Consider a pharmaceutical executive who knows that a major drug trial has failed. Under current law, this information remains hidden until formal disclosure, during which time uninformed investors continue trading at inflated prices. If insider trading were legal, the executive's selling would immediately begin pushing the price downward, signaling problems to the market and protecting other investors from buying at artificially high prices.

This price adjustment mechanism works in both directions. Positive inside information leads to buying that raises prices, while negative information triggers selling that lowers them. In both cases, the market price moves closer to reality sooner, reducing the period during which stocks trade at incorrect valuations. This benefits all market participants by providing more accurate pricing signals for investment decisions.

The Compensation and Innovation Argument

Legalizing insider trading would create a powerful, market-based compensation mechanism for corporate entrepreneurs and innovators. In many companies, especially startups and high-tech firms, the individuals who create value through innovation have intimate knowledge of their breakthroughs before public announcement. Allowing them to profit from this knowledge through trading provides direct rewards for value creation without requiring complex compensation committees or subjective performance evaluations.

This form of compensation is self-regulating and automatically scaled to the value created. An executive whose decisions genuinely increase firm value can profit proportionally, while those whose insider information reveals problems suffer losses if they own shares. This creates better alignment between management interests and corporate performance than current compensation structures, which often reward executives regardless of actual value creation.

The Victimless Transaction Argument

Critics of insider trading struggle to identify actual victims. In modern anonymous markets, buyers and sellers transact with willing counterparties who have already decided to trade. The investor selling shares to an insider buying on positive information was already planning to sell—the insider's purchase doesn't cause their loss, but merely determines who receives their shares. Similarly, someone buying from an insider selling on negative information had already decided to buy at that price.

The notion that insider trading "harms" other investors confuses correlation with causation. Yes, those trading opposite to insiders may experience opportunity costs, but these same costs exist whenever anyone trades on superior analysis, better technology, or faster information processing—all perfectly legal activities. The market has always rewarded information advantages; arbitrarily criminalizing one category of information while permitting others lacks logical consistency.

The Enforcement Problem: Wasted Resources and Arbitrary Prosecution

Current insider trading enforcement consumes enormous regulatory and judicial resources while yielding questionable benefits. The SEC and Department of Justice spend millions annually investigating and prosecuting insider trading cases, resources that could address genuine fraud and market manipulation. The complexity of these cases, often requiring years of investigation and litigation, demonstrates the difficulty of even defining what constitutes illegal insider trading.

Moreover, enforcement is necessarily selective and arguably arbitrary. For every insider trading case prosecuted, countless similar transactions go undetected or unprosecuted. This creates a system where punishment depends more on chance or political considerations than actual harm caused. Such arbitrary enforcement undermines respect for law and creates uncertainty that itself harms market efficiency.

Property Rights in Information

Information is a form of property, and those who create or legitimately acquire valuable information should have the right to profit from it. Current insider trading laws essentially confiscate this property right, forcing information holders to give away valuable knowledge for free. This resembles requiring a gold prospector to announce his discovery before staking his claim—it destroys incentives for information production and discovery.

If a firm believes restricting insider trading benefits shareholders, it can implement and enforce such restrictions through employment contracts. Critics argue that legalizing insider trading would reduce market participation by destroying confidence in market fairness. The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Enhancing Market Efficiency and Economic Prosperity

Introduction

Insider trading remains one of the most contentious issues in financial regulation, yet the conventional wisdom prohibiting it deserves rigorous reconsideration. This essay argues that fully legalizing insider trading would enhance market efficiency, benefit investors, and serve the broader public interest. The central thesis is straightforward: allowing insiders to trade on material non-public information accelerates the incorporation of that information into stock prices, leading to more accurate asset valuations and superior capital allocation throughout the economy.

The Efficiency Argument: Faster Price Discovery

The fundamental benefit of legalizing insider trading lies in improved market efficiency. When insiders trade on private information, they move prices toward their true fundamental values more quickly than would otherwise occur. This rapid price adjustment serves several crucial functions:

First, it provides more accurate signals to all market participants. When a stock price reflects insider knowledge about upcoming earnings, technological breakthroughs, or pending disasters, other investors can make better-informed decisions even without knowing the specific information. The price itself becomes an information aggregator.

Second, expedited price discovery reduces the period during which securities trade at incorrect valuations. Currently, material information may remain private for weeks or months before public disclosure. During this time, uninformed investors trade at prices disconnected from reality. Insider trading would compress this inefficiency window significantly.

Third, accurate pricing facilitates optimal capital allocation. When stock prices rapidly reflect company prospects, capital flows more efficiently to promising enterprises and away from failing ones. This benefits overall economic productivity.

Challenging the Fairness Objection

Critics claim insider trading is "unfair" to ordinary investors, but this objection crumbles under scrutiny. Markets are inherently characterized by information asymmetries. Professional analysts, institutional investors, and sophisticated traders consistently profit from superior research, expertise, and resources. We don't ban these advantages because we recognize that informed trading improves price accuracy.

Insider trading represents merely another form of information advantage—one that happens to be particularly valuable for price discovery. The insider's counterparty isn't harmed in any meaningful sense; they planned to trade anyway at prevailing prices. The presence of an informed insider actually benefits them by ensuring those prices more accurately reflect underlying value.

Furthermore, if insider trading were legal and expected, market prices would adjust to incorporate this reality. Bid-ask spreads might widen slightly to compensate for increased adverse selection, but this cost would be offset by the substantial benefits of improved price accuracy.

Property Rights and Entrepreneurial Compensation

Insider trading rights could function as efficient property rights over information. Pioneer legal scholar Henry Manne argued that allowing insider trading provides optimal compensation for entrepreneurial executives whose innovations create corporate value. Traditional compensation methods (salaries, bonuses, stock options) often fail to adequately reward the executives whose insights and decisions generate the most value.

When an executive can trade on knowledge of their own successful innovations, they capture returns proportional to the value created. This creates powerful incentives for innovation and value-creating activities. Companies could explicitly negotiate insider trading rights as part of compensation packages, allowing markets to determine the optimal allocation of these information property rights.

Reducing Regulatory Costs and Burdens

The current prohibition on insider trading imposes enormous costs: extensive SEC enforcement apparatus, costly compliance programs at every public company, frequent litigation, and criminal prosecutions. These resources could be deployed more productively elsewhere.

Moreover, insider trading laws suffer from inherent vagueness. What constitutes "material" information? When does someone become a "temporary insider"? These ambiguities create legal uncertainty, chill legitimate business communications, and enable selective prosecution. Legalization would eliminate these inefficiencies.

Enhanced Corporate Monitoring

Legal insider trading would provide another benefit: improved corporate monitoring. If executives could trade freely, their trading patterns would serve as powerful signals about company performance. Unusual selling might indicate problems before they become catastrophic. Heavy buying would signal confidence in new initiatives.

Currently, executives face such stringent restrictions that their trading conveys minimal information. Legal insider trading would transform insider transactions into valuable information sources for analysts, regulators, and investors.

Addressing the Disclosure Alternative

Some argue that enhanced disclosure requirements provide a superior alternative to legalizing insider trading. However, mandatory disclosure has significant limitations. Companies often have legitimate reasons to keep information confidential temporarily—ongoing negotiations, competitive considerations, or incomplete developments. Forcing premature disclosure can harm companies and shareholders.

Insider trading offers a middle path: information reaches market prices without requiring public disclosure that might harm corporate interests. The price adjusts while the specific information remains confidential, protecting legitimate business interests while improving market efficiency.

International Competitiveness

Many jurisdictions have historically maintained more permissive approaches to insider trading, often with minimal apparent harm. Some emerging markets with relatively lax enforcement continue experiencing robust growth. While the United States has pursued aggressive insider trading prohibition, it's unclear whether this policy has generated net benefits compared to more relaxed alternatives.

Liberalizing insider trading rules could enhance U.S. market competitiveness by reducing regulatory burdens on companies and investors while maintaining the information efficiency that makes American capital markets attractive.

Conclusion

The case for legalizing insider trading rests on solid economic foundations. By accelerating the incorporation of private information into market prices, insider trading enhances market efficiency—the central function of securities markets. The supposed unfairness to ordinary investors dissolves upon examination, revealing itself as merely another information asymmetry in markets characterized by countless such asymmetries.

Additional benefits include superior entrepreneurial incentives, reduced regulatory costs, improved corporate monitoring, and enhanced market competitiveness. While this position challenges conventional wisdom, it deserves serious consideration from policymakers willing to prioritize economic efficiency and genuine market function over simplistic notions of fairness.

The prohibition on insider trading represents regulatory overreach based more on intuition and populist sentiment than rigorous economic analysis. As we continue refining financial regulation, we should be willing to reconsider whether this particular prohibition serves the public interest—or whether legalization would better serve investors, companies, and the broader economy.

The Forbidden Catalyst: Why Legalizing Insider Trading is the Key to Market Efficiency

The term "insider trading" evokes powerful images of corruption: shadowy figures in pinstripe suits exploiting secret knowledge for illicit gain at the expense of the ordinary public. This perception has been meticulously cultivated and is enshrined in a complex web of securities laws designed to ensure a "level playing field." However, this emotionally charged view obscures a profound economic truth: the current prohibition on insider trading is not a bulwark protecting market integrity, but a regulatory failure that actively impedes the market's most critical function—the efficient pricing of capital. A rigorous examination of financial theory and practical outcomes reveals that the full legalization of insider trading would not be an endorsement of corruption, but a sophisticated policy choice to enhance market efficiency by drastically accelerating the incorporation of material, non-public information into stock prices.

The foundational argument for legalization rests on the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), which posits that stock prices reflect all available information. The faster and more accurately information is embedded into a stock's price, the more efficiently capital is allocated throughout the economy. Capital flows to its most productive uses, fostering innovation and growth. The current legal regime creates a significant lag—an "information friction"—between when corporate insiders learn something material and when the market is permitted to know it. Executives, directors, and key employees are often privy to groundbreaking innovations, disastrous product failures, or seismic shifts in quarterly earnings long before public disclosure. Under the present system, they are forced to remain silent, and the market continues to trade based on outdated or incomplete data. This means a company on the verge of a bankruptcy-causing scandal may be wildly overvalued, while a company with a revolutionary, undisclosed breakthrough remains undervalued. This mispricing leads to a profound misallocation of society's scarce capital resources.

Legalizing insider trading would eliminate this friction by creating a powerful, immediate, and unambiguous mechanism for information dissemination: the trade itself. If a CEO confidentially learns that her company's new drug has received FDA approval, she has a strong incentive to purchase shares. Her market order to buy, especially if it is a large and unusual trade, sends a powerful signal to the market. Astute analysts and institutional investors would detect this unusual buying activity and investigate, gradually deducing the positive news. The act of trading itself becomes a form of communication, and the stock price would begin to climb, reflecting the new reality long before a formal press release is drafted and disseminated. Conversely, if a CFO discovers an enormous accounting fraud, his urgent sale of stock would be a deafening alarm bell, quickly driving the price down to a level that more accurately reflects the company's perilous state. In both scenarios, the price becomes a more truthful and timely signal, enabling all market participants—even those unaware of the specific news—to make decisions based on a more accurate valuation.

Opponents of legalization inevitably raise the specter of a catastrophic loss of public confidence. They argue that if the "little guy" perceives the market as a rigged game where insiders always win, he will refuse to participate, draining the markets of the liquidity they need to function. This argument, while intuitively appealing, is flawed on two counts. First, it presumes the current system is not already rigged. The reality is that a form of legalized insider trading already exists. Corporate insiders can and do legally trade their own company's stock by filing pre-scheduled trading plans (10b5-1 plans). While designed to prevent abuse, these plans can be gamed. More importantly, a vast information asymmetry persists between sophisticated Wall Street institutions with teams of analysts conducting "channel checks" and the average retail investor. The market has never been a perfectly level field; the question is whether we prefer a system where information trickles out slowly and opaquely or one where it is rapidly incorporated into prices through transparent action.

Second, the "public confidence" argument underestimates the rationality of investors. Most participants understand they are at an informational disadvantage; they invest in index funds or rely on professional money managers for this very reason. Their primary concern is not whether someone else has better information, but whether the price they are paying for a stock is fair. A market where prices rapidly adjust to reflect all information, including that traded on by insiders, is by definition a fairer and more reliable market for determining value. The confidence of a rational investor should be bolstered, not undermined, by knowing that the price on their screen is a more real-time and accurate reflection of a company's true worth.

Furthermore, legalization would create a more robust system of corporate accountability. Imagine if executives knew their trades would be immediately scrutinized as signals of company health. A sudden, large-scale sell-off by the C-suite would act as a devastating vote of no confidence, potentially cratering the stock price and bringing immediate scrutiny from the board and shareholders. This would serve as a powerful check on managerial malfeasance, forcing executives to be far more transparent and accountable for their performance. The market itself would become a relentless auditor.

In conclusion, the demonization of insider trading is a political and moral stance, not an economic one. It is based on an outdated ideal of fairness that ultimately creates more inefficiency, more mispricing, and a slower, less responsive market. By fully legalizing the practice, we would not be unleashing chaos but embracing a more sophisticated and rational market mechanism. We would be empowering the most powerful force in capitalism—accurate price signals—to work faster and more effectively. The resulting market would be more efficient, more transparent in its operations, and a superior allocator of the capital that drives human progress. It is time to repeal the well-intentioned but economically destructive prohibitions and allow the market to process all information, by any means necessary, with the urgency it demands.

Core Free-Market Principle: The Hayekian Argument

The foundational argument stems from the work of Nobel laureate economist Friedrich Hayek. Hayek posited that information in society is not centralized; it is dispersed, fragmented, and held by countless individuals. The price system in a free market is a marvel because it aggregates this dispersed information into a single, meaningful signal: the market price.

From this view, insiders are simply individuals with a crucial fragment of information. Preventing them from trading is effectively hindering that information from being incorporated into the stock price. Legalizing their trades would allow this valuable, hidden information to flow into the market much more quickly.

How Legalized Insider Trading Could Improve Price Discovery

Price discovery is the process by which market prices adjust to reflect all available information. Proponents argue that insider trading accelerates this process dramatically.

  1. Speed of Information Incorporation: Insiders (e.g., a CEO, a lead scientist) know about a major development—a breakthrough product, a failed clinical trial, a pending merger—long before it can be legally announced and digested by the public. If they are allowed to trade on this information, their buying or selling pressure will immediately begin moving the stock price. The market might not know the reason, but it will see the effect: "There's unusual buying volume in this stock; smart money must know something." The price begins to correct toward its "true" value immediately, rather than waiting for a formal press release weeks or months later.

  2. More Accurate Prices: A stock price that reflects both public and soon-to-be-public information is a more accurate signal of the company's true fundamental value. This accuracy is crucial for the efficient allocation of capital in the economy. Investors are less likely to over-invest in a company hiding failures or under-invest in a company with secret successes if the price more accurately reflects reality.

How It Could Enhance Overall Market Efficiency

Market efficiency means that prices fully reflect all available information. The strong form of the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) controversially suggests that even insider information is reflected in prices. Legalizing insider trading would be a mechanism to make the strong form of EMH a reality.

  1. Incentivizes Information Discovery: The potential for profit is a powerful incentive. If insiders can profit from their superior knowledge, they are incentivized to seek out that knowledge more diligently and act on it more quickly. This creates a constant, powerful force pushing prices toward their fundamental value. Academics like Henry Manne (in his seminal book Insider Trading and the Stock Market, 1966) argued that insider trading is actually a compensation mechanism for entrepreneurs and innovators. It rewards them for creating valuable information (e.g., a new innovation) that benefits society, much like a patent does.

  2. Liquidity and the "Greater Fool" Theory: Contrary to the intuition that it hurts ordinary investors, some argue it protects them. In a world where insider trading is illegal, unsuspecting retail investors might be the "greater fools" buying stock from an insider who knows the company is about to crash but cannot trade. If insiders could trade, their selling would drive the price down before the bad news is public, warning other investors away from an overvalued asset. The people selling to the insiders (who are buying before good news) are voluntarily parting with their shares at a price they find acceptable, based on the information they have.

  3. Reduces the Advantage of Large Institutions: The current system is not perfectly fair. Large institutional investors have armies of analysts who can piece together non-public information from supply chains, satellite images, and channel checks (so-called "mosaic theory"). This is legal. An individual insider might have a clearer, more definitive piece of information but is barred from acting. Legalization could, in theory, level the playing field between corporate insiders and financial industry insiders.

Important Counterarguments and Nuances

It is crucial to note that these are theoretical benefits from a specific economic perspective. The reality is far more complex, and the policy is overwhelmingly rejected for strong reasons:

  • Erosion of Trust: The primary counterargument is that markets require trust. If investors believe the game is rigged and that insiders constantly have an unassailable advantage, they will withdraw their capital. This reduces market participation, liquidity, and ultimately increases the cost of capital for companies, harming everyone.

A CEO might forgo a beneficial long-term project to engineer a short-term price drop to buy shares cheaply, or delay good news to load up on stock first. This damages the principle that executives should act as fiduciaries for all shareholders.

The insider is a steward of that property. To use it for personal gain is a form of theft or breach of fiduciary duty, which is a violation of contract and property rights—core tenets of free-market economics.

From a pure, theoretical free-market economics perspective, the case for legalizing insider trading rests on the idea that information is the lifeblood of markets and should not be artificially stifled. Allowing those with information to trade ensures that prices become accurate, efficient signals faster, which leads to a better allocation of resources across the entire economy. It is framed not as a cheat code for the privileged, but as the most efficient mechanism for incorporating hidden knowledge into market prices, benefiting society through more efficient markets.

However, in practice, the perceived injustices and the potential for severe agency problems have led every major developed market to ban the practice, prioritizing market integrity and participant trust over theoretical gains in pricing efficiency.

The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: A Market Efficiency Argument

Introduction

Few propositions in financial regulation provoke as visceral a reaction as the suggestion that insider trading should be legal. The practice—broadly defined as trading securities on the basis of material, nonpublic information—has been vilified in popular culture, prosecuted aggressively by the Securities and Exchange Commission, and treated as a self-evident moral wrong by politicians on both sides of the aisle. Yet beneath the reflexive outrage lies an intellectually serious and historically rich argument that deserves rigorous examination: allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices, and the legal apparatus constructed to prevent it produces costs that far exceed any benefits it confers. This essay argues that insider trading should be fully legalized, drawing on economic theory, empirical evidence, and philosophical principles of free exchange.

I. The Foundational Argument: Information and Market Efficiency

A. The Efficient Market Hypothesis and the Information Problem

The cornerstone of modern financial economics is the Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH), articulated most famously by Eugene Fama in 1970. In its strongest form, the EMH holds that stock prices reflect all available information—public and private. In its semi-strong form, prices reflect all publicly available information. Most regulators operate under the assumption that markets should aspire to at least semi-strong efficiency, believing that keeping insider information out of trading somehow protects the integrity of the pricing mechanism.

But this reasoning is paradoxical. If the goal of a well-functioning securities market is to produce prices that accurately reflect the true underlying value of a company, then any barrier to the flow of information into prices is, by definition, a barrier to efficiency. Insider trading prohibitions do not prevent material information from existing; they merely delay the point at which that information is reflected in the price of a security. The result is that stock prices remain inaccurate for longer than they otherwise would, and investors who trade during the period of ignorance are, ironically, the very people the law claims to protect.

B. Henry Manne and the Intellectual Foundation

The most rigorous academic case for legalizing insider trading was made by Professor Henry Manne in his landmark 1966 book Insider Trading and the Stock Market. Manne argued that insider trading is the most efficient mechanism available for moving stock prices toward their correct values. When a corporate executive learns that her company has discovered a breakthrough pharmaceutical compound, her purchases of the company's stock begin to push the price upward before any public announcement. This price movement sends a signal to the market—a signal that, while imprecise, nudges the stock closer to its true post-announcement value.

Without insider trading, the stock price remains artificially stagnant, mispricing the security and misleading every investor who buys or sells during the information gap. Far from being a form of theft, insider trading is an act of information transmission—a service to the market and to the investing public.

C. The Speed of Price Discovery

Consider the mechanics more carefully. When insiders trade, their activity generates observable phenomena: unusual volume, price movement, and shifts in the options market. Sophisticated market participants—analysts, quantitative traders, algorithmic systems—detect these patterns and trade accordingly, even without knowing the specific information that motivated the insider's trade. This cascading process accelerates price discovery, reducing the window during which a stock is mispriced.

Empirical research supports this mechanism. A study by Meulbroek (1992) found that nearly half of the stock price run-up preceding takeover announcements occurred on days with detected insider trading, demonstrating that insider activity meaningfully contributed to price adjustment before public disclosure. Cornell and Sirri (1992) documented a similar pattern, finding that insider trading around the acquisition of Campbell Taggart by Anheuser-Busch moved prices toward their post-announcement equilibrium well in advance of public knowledge. Legalizing this activity would not create a new phenomenon; it would simply remove the legal penalties that currently make the phenomenon covert, sporadic, and less effective than it could be.

II. The Failure of Prohibition

A. Enforcement Is Arbitrary and Expensive

The prohibition of insider trading in the United States rests on a remarkably unstable legal foundation. Unlike most securities violations, insider trading has never been defined by statute. The SEC prosecutes it under the broad anti-fraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5, relying on judicial theories—the "classical theory," the "misappropriation theory," and the "tipper-tippee" framework—that have evolved through decades of inconsistent case law. The result is a body of regulation that even securities lawyers struggle to interpret with confidence.

The Supreme Court's tortured jurisprudence in cases from Chiarella v. United States (1980) to Salman v. United States (2016) illustrates the problem. The boundaries of liability shift depending on the relationship between the trader and the source of information, the nature of any "personal benefit" conferred on the tipper, and the trader's awareness of the breach of fiduciary duty. This legal uncertainty imposes enormous compliance costs on corporations, financial institutions, and individual investors, all of whom must navigate a regulatory minefield with indistinct borders.

Meanwhile, enforcement is inevitably selective. The SEC brings roughly 50 to 60 insider trading cases per year in a market where millions of trades occur daily. Given the difficulty of detecting and proving insider trading, the prohibition functions less as a genuine deterrent and more as an arbitrary tax on the unlucky or unsophisticated few who are caught. The vast majority of informed trading—including trading by corporate insiders who carefully structure their transactions to stay within legal safe harbors—goes undetected and unpunished. The pretense of prohibition creates an illusion of fairness while the underlying reality remains unchanged.

B. The Ban Does Not Eliminate Information Asymmetry

Proponents of insider trading laws often argue that they "level the playing field" for ordinary investors. This claim does not survive scrutiny. Information asymmetry is an inherent and ineradicable feature of securities markets. Professional analysts, institutional investors, and high-frequency traders all possess informational advantages over retail investors—advantages derived from superior research, faster technology, and privileged access to management through earnings calls, investor days, and private meetings.

The distinction between "legal" informational advantages and "illegal" insider trading is, in many cases, one of degree rather than kind. An analyst who develops a proprietary model predicting a company's earnings with uncanny accuracy is rewarded for her informational edge. A portfolio manager who reads body language during a private meeting with a CEO and adjusts his position accordingly faces no legal jeopardy. But a mid-level employee who trades on concrete knowledge of the same earnings figure before its release is a criminal. The moral logic underlying this distinction is far less obvious than regulators would have us believe.

By legalizing insider trading, we would at least ensure that informational advantages are translated into price signals rather than hoarded. A world in which insiders trade freely is a world in which their knowledge reaches the market faster, reducing—not increasing—the disadvantage faced by uninformed investors.

III. Insider Trading as Efficient Compensation

A. Aligning Incentives

One of Manne's most compelling arguments was that insider trading could serve as an efficient form of entrepreneurial compensation. Corporate managers and employees who create value—by developing new products, negotiating profitable deals, or identifying cost savings—possess information about the value they have created before the market does. Allowing them to trade on that information permits them to capture a portion of the value they generate, aligning their incentives with shareholder interests more precisely than many formal compensation schemes.

Stock options and restricted stock units, the primary tools of modern executive compensation, are blunt instruments. They reward executives for general stock price appreciation that may have nothing to do with the executive's performance—a rising tide lifts all boats. They also create perverse incentives to manipulate the timing of disclosures to maximize option value. Insider trading, by contrast, rewards specific acts of value creation at the moment they occur, providing a more granular and accurate form of performance-based compensation.

B. Reducing Agency Costs

The corporate governance literature is replete with analyses of the "agency problem"—the divergence of interests between managers and shareholders. Allowing insiders to trade aligns these interests directly and continuously, rather than through the crude and manipulable mechanisms of annual bonuses and long-term incentive plans. An executive who knows she can profit from good decisions and will suffer losses from bad ones (since she can trade on both positive and negative information) has a powerful, self-enforcing incentive to maximize firm value.

Critics object that insider trading on negative information—selling before bad news—creates an incentive for managers to destroy value. But this concern is overblown. Managers who deliberately damage their companies face consequences far more severe than trading losses: termination, reputational destruction, and potential liability for breach of fiduciary duty. The marginal profit from short-selling one's employer's stock is trivial compared to the career-ending consequences of being identified as the source of a company's decline.

IV. Addressing the Fairness Objection

A. The Illusion of Equal Access

The most emotionally powerful argument against insider trading is the fairness argument: it is simply "unfair" for someone to profit from information that other investors do not possess. But this argument, while intuitive, is philosophically and economically incoherent.

All profit in a market economy arises from differential knowledge, skill, or effort. A farmer who understands soil conditions better than his neighbor profits from that knowledge. A venture capitalist who identifies a promising startup before others do profits from her superior judgment. A trader who develops a faster algorithm profits from his technological investment. In no other domain of economic life do we criminalize the use of superior information. The securities market is not a charity or a public utility; it is a mechanism for aggregating information and allocating capital. Its purpose is served, not undermined, when better-informed participants move prices toward accuracy.

Moreover, the "fairness" argument implicitly assumes that uninformed investors are harmed by insider trading. But in an anonymous market, the counterparty to an insider's trade is not a specific victim; it is whoever happened to be on the other side of the transaction. That person was going to trade regardless of the insider's participation—their order was already in the market. The insider's trade does not cause the counterparty's loss; the counterparty's loss is a function of the information gap that would have existed whether or not the insider traded. Indeed, by moving the price closer to its true value, the insider's trade reduces the magnitude of losses for investors who would otherwise have traded at an even more inaccurate price.

B. Comparative Institutional Analysis

We should also consider the alternative to insider trading: a regime in which material information is hoarded inside corporations until the moment of public disclosure, at which point the stock price adjusts violently. This regime does not protect unsophisticated investors; it exposes them to dramatic price swings that they are least equipped to handle. A gradual price adjustment—facilitated by insider trading—is more forgiving to retail investors than the abrupt, all-at-once corrections that characterize our current disclosure-based system.

Furthermore, the prohibition of insider trading does not eliminate informed trading; it merely drives it underground, where it benefits only those willing to break the law. Legalization would democratize the information transmission function, allowing corporate insiders to trade openly and transparently, with their transactions visible to all market participants through mandatory disclosure filings.

V. International and Historical Perspective

It is worth noting that the aggressive American approach to insider trading enforcement is not universal. Many countries have adopted insider trading prohibitions only recently, and enforcement varies dramatically across jurisdictions. Prior to the European Union's Market Abuse Directive, several European countries treated insider trading as a minor regulatory infraction rather than a serious crime. Japan's enforcement of insider trading laws has historically been minimal. In many emerging markets, insider trading laws exist on paper but are rarely enforced.

Yet these markets have not collapsed. Investors continue to allocate capital, companies continue to raise funds, and economies continue to grow. The empirical evidence does not support the claim that insider trading prohibitions are necessary for the functioning of capital markets. To the contrary, the most liquid and efficient market in the world—the United States—is also the one where insider trading is most prevalent, despite being the most aggressively prosecuted. This paradox suggests that the economic incentives for informed trading are so powerful that no regulatory regime can suppress them, and that the attempt to do so merely imposes deadweight costs on the system.

VI. The Path Forward: A Framework for Legal Insider Trading

Legalization need not mean deregulation. A sensible framework for legal insider trading would include several elements:

  1. Mandatory Disclosure: Insiders would be required to report trades within 24 hours (as they already must under Section 16 of the Securities Exchange Act), providing transparency and enabling the market to draw inferences from insider activity.

  2. Contractual Regulation: Companies would be free to restrict insider trading through employment agreements and corporate governance policies. If a board of directors believes that insider trading by its executives is harmful to the firm, it can prohibit it as a condition of employment. This allows firm-specific optimization rather than one-size-fits-all federal regulation.

  3. Fraud Preservation: Legalization of insider trading would not eliminate liability for affirmative fraud. If an insider trades on the basis of information she has fabricated, or if she manipulates the market through false statements, existing anti-fraud provisions would continue to apply.

  4. Fiduciary Duty Constraints: Corporate officers and directors would remain subject to state-law fiduciary duties, ensuring that their trading does not constitute self-dealing at the expense of the corporation.

This framework preserves the core benefits of insider trading—accelerated price discovery, efficient compensation, and reduced information asymmetry—while addressing legitimate concerns about disclosure and corporate governance.

VII. Conclusion

The prohibition of insider trading is one of the most deeply entrenched orthodoxies in American financial regulation. It enjoys broad political support, widespread public approval, and the passionate advocacy of regulators who have built careers on its enforcement. But orthodoxy is not argument, and popularity is not proof.

Allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices. It produces more accurate security valuations, benefits uninformed investors by narrowing the window of mispricing, provides efficient and self-calibrating compensation for value-creating employees, and reduces the deadweight costs of a regulatory apparatus that is arbitrary in its application and futile in its ambitions. The fairness concerns that motivate the prohibition are philosophically confused and empirically unsupported.

The intellectual case for legalization, first articulated by Henry Manne nearly six decades ago, has only grown stronger as financial markets have become more complex, more global, and more dependent on the rapid flow of information. It is time to move beyond the morality play of insider trading prosecutions and toward a regulatory framework that embraces the fundamental insight of market economics: prices are most useful when they are most accurate, and they are most accurate when information flows freely. Legalizing insider trading is not a concession to greed; it is a commitment to the principle that well-informed markets serve everyone better than ignorant ones.

Note: This essay presents an academic argument from a specific economic perspective. Insider trading is currently illegal in the United States and most jurisdictions. Allocation of Capital

  • Optimal Resource Allocation: Accurate pricing ensures that capital flows to its most productive uses. Companies with strong prospects are more likely to attract investment, while weaker companies face appropriate market discipline.

Liquidity Enhancement

  • Increased Trading Activity: The prospect of trading on insider information can lead to increased market participation. More participants and trades generally improve market liquidity, making it easier for all investors to buy and sell securities without significantly affecting prices.
